entry.title: The story behind my internet name
entry.content:
@TheDataAreClean

Part #1: Plurality

When I say the word “data”, what comes to your mind?

Do you think of one body of information or many individual pieces? This has been a point of low-to-mild contention in the data world for years. I land on the plural side of the argument.

Technically speaking, data is the plural form of the Latin word datum, meaning “a single piece of information”. So I write sentences like “The data are ready for analysis” or “Many of these data were collected over years”.

That is where the first part of my internet name comes from: thedataare.

There is also this strip about the same topic from PhD Comics.

Part #2: Insanity

“Does this job have analytics?”

“When will I do data science?”

“I want to work on models.”

In the early years of my career, I would hear these questions regularly, often weekly, from interns and young professionals working with me. Every time, I felt intense rage at hearing some version of them.

So many of these new joiners had gone through prohibitively expensive and extremely useless data science boot camps. They had been shown an ideal world where a magical stork delivers a dataset and they get straight to “building models” and “doing machine learning”.

Somewhere between the expectations those boot camps had set and the pointless conversations we were having, the most fundamental questions kept getting left out. Where does the data come from? What happens once you have it? How do you use it to understand something?

I would keep asking them, do you even understand your data well enough to make these assumptions? To run these so-called “models”? Never got a convincing answer to my questions, and the interns would try to do what they want anyway. When the results made no sense, they seemed to think they were missing some secret sauce for analysing the data. It was rarely questioned how little they knew about the data itself.

I often point out the importance of getting to know the data, spending time with it, and cleaning it before attempting even the simplest analysis. That frustration is where the “clean” in thedataareclean comes from.

Even today, understanding and cleaning the data remain the most important part of any analysis for me.

The good part

There are perks to having such an unusual internet name. I can find and claim the handle pretty much anywhere, even when I am very late to a platform.

Written in response to:

What’s the story behind your domain name? (Or your government name, or your online handle.)

– Prompt from IndieWebClub Bangalore meetup #36.

entry.title: [Weeknotes] Week of 24th October, 2026: fomo at work, inflammation management
entry.content:
Work

I was hoping to spend this week working on gaining an intuition for the layers in which building observability is natural and useful. Unfortunately I spent half a day on this, and then had to go back to evals work (which I love! But I was looking forward to the new thing) involving the math around runs, intuiting noise in a run, separating out each grader into its constituent parts, etc. Except then I couldn't even do that properly because I was sick most of the week. We're moving on to a new prototype at work in the midst of this and I've had lots of fomo and been annoyed because being sick has kept me out of lots of fun conversations and work.

I'm mildly stuck on a few blog posts: two for evals, the giant that is the delhi blog post, and a few more in my head. Posts and post ideas come easy to me these days, i just need to make the time for it.

Health

I had an itch in my throat starting Wednesday morning and so I did everything in my power to make things better. Updated the care document with some of this because I had forgotten the order and all the options available to me. I think I escaped the worst of it (mostly no fever) but I had really bad low BP spells and needed to be handed food once which was embarrassing and annoying.

I also had to go to my allergist because appointments are very hard to come by. The appointment was for just I was recovering and unfortunately I think it really set me back :( more bad news is that I'm not responding as well as I should to the immunology treatment. That's likely because of my body's propensity to be inflammed... But this means i need to now get back into micromanaging it and that thought is exhausting. For example, i might have to go back to gfdf.

\*gets on the floor and kicks and screams\*

One good thing this week has been that I have confirmed how good and easy a simple thing like looking up on YouTube 10 minute yoga routine for when you're sick is for my body. I also did some cooking because I was being specific in my desires for soup.

Life

Last weekend was really social! I am posting this weeknote at this time entirely because of the tareefen i got from going to iwc last Saturday after posting that one 😁

I went to a gig at social Saturday night because a friend was organising it and another friend was DJing! I was really tired and almost didn't go but a third friend who never dances and rarely does gigs promised to dance with me so I couldn't say no. And I went. It was tiring, I had fun, met so many familiar faces after a while (including at the after party!) but my god... fuck social indiranagar. Of the 12 people I know and met, 8 -eight!!!!- have fallen sick. I didn't even drink!!! Very, very mad about this. I will be avoiding social indiranagar gigs where I can moving forward - if I can't (i do want to support artists friend and producer friends etc) i will not even be drinking water there (because that's really all I did).

Other lowlights:

cancelled 4 different casual social hangs on account of sickness and infectiousness.

Someone I knew from the regular community/dev/tech policy circuit passed away earlier this week. I didn't know them well, but they have been a fixture in the scene since I was 20 years old. it feels a little surreal that they won't be around any more. It feels most surreal because I met them two weeks ago! They came to Recurse Center co-working and talked about a proposal they were writing and work they have been wanting to do. And just like that, they're gone now.

Im not sure how grief like this should be handled, or thought about. Im glad we talked about it and about him on the day of coworking as a group. Community is so important in helping regulate some of these things.

A friend is giving up their house and vagabonding for a few months. So at the end of this very long Tuesday, I had 16 boxes in my loft! I did none of the heavy lifting - literally. But it feels good to be able to offer home and space to people.

Learning

This heading feels a little superfluous now - because most of the effort I put into anything these days is learning. Ive made it so that I'm learning on the job more effectively and in parallel to execution. Same with any other kind of reading or hobbies I'm doing.

Media Diet

Listening

Chutney Mary played an Imogen Heap inspired set which tells me I need to listen to more of her. Daisho incorporated k pop into his very lush, drip set which I adored. There might be acid techno out there which works for me. I haven't found it yet but it might exist somewhere. New lisa album I'm pretty excited about. Really enjoyed exactly one The Avalanches album. Rohini told me about The Chicks - i can't believe I've just not listened to them before.

entry.title: Q&A for aspiring space writers
entry.content:
I recently did a short interview for The 19th Orbit, a newsletter started by the 19-year old Shashank Shekhar who is passionate about space and science communications. I was happy that he reached out. It’s always nice to hear from and know about readers of my space blog. Below are his questions and my answers, which I think could benefit others too wanting to launch similar efforts.

1. You were the Science Officer for TeamIndus’ lunar mission. What did that experience teach you about space missions and the gap between its technicalities and the public’s understanding?

This was an exciting period where I got to learn about and see first hand the anatomy of a space mission. I could talk to engineers across subsystems and understand how parts of a spacecraft are intertwined. I also interacted with planetary scientists advising and working with us, and part of my role involved relaying their needs to engineers. A lot of public communications about space missions did not and still do not cover such intricacies, sadly, which would otherwise help people even in the industry make better sense of space updates. This is why I ended up using that experience to start my Moon Monday blog+newsletter.

2. You’ve written for The Planetary Society, The Wire, and many more outlets worldwide. How do you balance scientific rigor with making space accessible to a general audience?

As one can imagine, it’s difficult compressing cutting-edge science and engineering developments into publicly readable pieces while also making sure you don’t compromise on accuracy. But that’s what makes the challenge intriguing and fun! That you can learn the essence of something during research and pass it on to the public who don’t necessarily have to go through the same steps is what makes the endeavor worthwhile. A lot of what I learnt and picked up about science communications for people at large is through writing articles under senior editors at various media publications and receiving their critical edits. What has also helped me is reading a lot, both science and non-science things, which gradually helps you express better in a given language. Relatedly, I’ve blogged about some basic writing tips, including how to avoid academic jargon. 

3. What advice would you give to a 19-year-old researcher in India who wants to build an independent voice in space writing?

Start a blog and post articles at any pace you’re able to. The platform doesn’t really matter. Don’t fret about monetizing your blog, at least not early on. Write and publish articles on your blog even if other media outlets or publications reject an idea. My now-popular article on India’s Mars orbiter mission was rejected 8 times but I published it anyway. Publications can teach you a lot, and you should pursue that route too, but they’re not the ultimate arbitrator of what needs to be published. The responsibility for the quality bar and depth of research is ultimately on you. Similarly, popularity does not equal quality. Social media will give you followers but it will not teach you how to write, or what is right.

entry.title: The Anthropologists
entry.content: Adheena recommended it, and I had also seen it on Obama’s list. It’s a small book in simple language, easy to finish in one sitting, but it deserves to be read slow. It reads like a list of fragmented notes from a narrator I couldn’t connect with much. It felt like reading her diary without permission, and at times I wanted to make sure she was not around. Like any diary, it is not about the narrator, but about what the writer sees and thinks. I could understand what she is going through, all her wandering and searching, and the people, the city and the situations felt very close to me and to people I know.

entry.title: Weeknote #37 [W43] - Return of the weeknote, looking for jobs, and dancing landscapes
entry.content:
Return of the weeknote, after 14 weeks of absence

My last weeknote was a while ago.

I don’t remember precisely why I had stopped. But somewhere in my mind I probably had this idea that I should write more stuff beyond weeknotes.

But stopping weeknotes, evidently, hasn’t helped with that goal.

So, after a bit of prodding from Tanvi (who has also resumed writing weeknotes recently), here we are again.

One of the benefits of writing weeknotes is that I remember the weeks I write about much better than the ones I don’t. So the last few months have certainly been blurrier than the rest of the year.

Looking for jobs

I completed a year at my current job two days ago.

I got stuck at my previous job for almost 5 years because it was rather comfortable. I don’t want to make that mistake again.

Switching jobs — and switching frequently — is probably the most reliable way to increase your salary. Particularly early in one’s career. This is because employers often use your previous salary to determine their offers (which sounds completely idiotic to me, but it is what it is). Staying in one place for too long can have a compounding cost.

So, for the last week or so, I’ve been applying to as many open Product Manager roles as I come across.

I don’t have a lot of experience with job hunting. I’ve managed to avoid actively looking for jobs until now. I’m generally far too lazy to go through the tedium that job searches entail (like making a CV, filling up a hundred forms, writing cover letters, and so on).

Friends and colleagues tell me that applying through job portals (LinkedIn and the likes) is mostly useless. What works, apparently, are referrals from within a company. It’s only been a bit more than a week, but my experience so far hasn’t given me any reason to disagree.

Maybe it is too early to conclude anything from these numbers. Most applications haven’t received a response yet. But a quick Google search tells me that apparently only 3% applications through jobs portals get a response.

Which probably means I should start “networking” more. I dread the idea more than how much my cat dreads his baths (which he has been getting frequently lately, by the way, because: fleas).

Dancing landscapes, and the benefits of LLMs

As a part of the job search, I finally “finished” my portfolio site for the first time ever.

It has been in various states of unfinished-ness for the past 6 years. (I find compiling a portfolio for myself rather tedious.) This time, I figured that I needed to add something more engaging to keep me from abandoning it yet again.

Around the time I started working on the portfolio again, I was also listening to Understanding Complexity, a lecture series on complexity theory by The Great Courses. (Worth checking out if you have an Audible subscription.)

One idea I came across was that of dancing landscapes. The idea is that a complex environment is like a landscape that is constantly changing with time. In such an environment, the path to achieving a goal changes along with the circumstances.

I found the idea interesting enough to build a page of interactive illustrations around it: Dancing landscapes. That page eventually became the anchor around which I rebuilt the portfolio. Having a smaller project I was actually interested in gave me a reason to stick with the larger project of finishing the portfolio.

I’ve never been very good with making animated data visualizations. I’ve used a bit of R and matplotlib on Python for a few projects in the past. But, as fun as it was, I never went back to it because there was no way to justify to myself the time it took to work on those things.

But we live in the age of LLMs now. And they are really good, and incredibly fast, at generating code.

I used to think that I liked writing code as a hobby. I’ve realized now that I probably didn’t. What I actually liked was creating aesthetically pleasing outcomes, and sometimes that meant writing code. (Which probably explains why I like CSS so much.)

Generating aesthetically pleasing outcomes from LLMs is still quite frustrating. The ratio of garbage to good output remains high. But the amount of tedium involved in reviewing LLM outputs and prompting them to get what you want is more tolerable to me than the tedium of writing code from scratch.

The results of LLM generated code have also improved way beyond anything I expected even 6 months ago. LLMs now write, on average, better code than what I or my colleagues at work would produce ourselves. We’ve reached a stage where we don’t read most of the code that goes into production, while also getting relatively fewer bugs than human written code (which was definitely not the case for us 6 months ago).

entry.title: Noodles with peanut butter sauce
entry.content:
If you like Maggi or instant noodles, please make this instead.

Takes almost the same amount of time and effort, but tastes exponentially better.

The peanut butter here gives the sauce a very rich, creamy and nutty base. Soy sauce adds umami and saltiness. Lime juice balances it out with tanginess and acidity. And the chilli oil adds some heat (and even more flavour).

Feel free to tweak the amounts to your liking. It is very difficult to get wrong.

Personally, I like it with more chilli oil than I’ve specified in the recipe.

Tips

  • Use smooth/creamy peanut butter if you can. I like to add crushed peanuts at the end, while serving, so that their retain their crunchiness and don’t get soggy.
  • The sauce thickens as it cools, so keep some of the noodle water handy to loosen it when needed.
  • It works great with a fried egg on top, and/or with pan seared prawns or chicken.

Ingredients

  • 150g Noodles (wheat or ramen)
  • 2 tbsp Peanut butter
  • 2 tbsp Soy sauce
  • 1 lime Lime juice
  • 3 tbsp Chilli oil
  • 2 tbsp Sesame oil
  • 2 cloves Garlic, minced
  • 2 Spring onions, chopped
  • 1 tbsp Crushed roasted peanuts

Method

  1. Bring a pot of salted water to a boil and cook the noodles for 8-10 minutes. Save about 1/4 cup of the cooking water before draining.
  2. While the noodles cook, whisk together the peanut butter, soy sauce, lime juice, chilli oil, sesame oil (or, optionally, fish oil), and garlic in a large bowl.
  3. Add the drained noodles to the bowl and toss until the noddles strand is coated. Add some hot water if needed to loosen the sauce.
  4. Taste and adjust with more soy sauce, lime juice, or chilli oil as needed.
  5. Serve topped with spring onions and crushed peanuts.

entry.title: Post Spar Debrief
entry.content:
I had been down with fever for a while and couldn't really go to the mma gym unless I wanted to start an outbreak.

Today was my first spar back after almost 2 weeks. Unfortunately I overslept and had to rush there so I didn't get the proper time to warm up.

The first fight went great, I was paired up with a newbie and I did not have shin guards, which was a bummer for me because while my shins are conditioned enough to not hurt when getting kicked but i can't kick the newbie hard unless I want him to quit the gym.

So with most of my arsenal locked I just had my punches and low kicks which I am used to practicing. I have gotten used to the rhythm of fighting people who don't really know how to throw a punch, it's very easy to predict when someone is throwing a blind haymaker with full power and it's also very easy to pop in and out of range to avoid getting hit. I am pretty decent at defence and I need more offensive practice.

My second fight was with a more experienced fighter and I can say that he's been putting in the work and made me work for whatever bits of ground I need to gain. Unfortunately I fucked up a bit while kicking him in the body by connecting my ankle with his elbow. This is a guy who can break coconuts open with his elbow which is a weird flex in the mma community, so now I'm paying for that mistake with an ankle that hurts immensely. I hope it's not broken, but c'est la vie.

Third round again with the newbie and he was getting angry at me for reason, and it really sucks when you let the emotions get to you. I understand his frustration of not being able to hit me, while I'm getting in and out of range counter punching his face, it is annoying as hell being on the other side. Hopefully he learns to be patient and not keep his big forehead out for me to punch.

My jab cross low kick combo is nearly perfect and my distance management is getting better. I know when I am in range and out of range. But the problem is that I need to get more creative with my combos. I need to incorporate more hooks, uppercuts, thrust kicks and spinning heel kicks. It makes my fights look more flashy and let's me set up unexpected situations.

I want to work on my pressure fighting but it can't be done with a newb because wild haymakers are a pain in the ass to deal with and I am not interested in getting knocked out on a Saturday morning because someone can't keep their ego in check.

I wish my ankle feels better tomorrow :(

entry.title: In Which I Suspect Bombay’s Cats of Foul Play
entry.content:
Cat distribution system.

Feline domination.

World of cats.

One more sentence to safeguard my work against being considered AI.

These are conspiracy theories I usually ignore because I got over cats taking over the internet long ago. Oh look, a cat does stupid shit. After seven years of scooping them, the shit stops being cute. Yeah, okay, man. Cats and stuff. Woo hoo. Eat your cake and have mine too.

But I’ve been spending a longer-than-anticipated time in Bombay, and I can no longer ignore the cats.

Allow me to preface this by saying that I have one and a half cat companions. The half is a cat that my feline companion adopted overnight, without consultation, consideration for my living space, or regard for my unemployment status. I therefore have “skin (scratched) in the game”—the game being my own blog post and my annoyance at this term, overused by Bangalore tech bros as a placeholder for “I can’t ask you to, but please work overtime without pay on this AI product I’m definitely building that I definitely don’t understand.”

This piece is going to have unjustified, hoity tangents, and many arguments are going to be a stretch. It is about cats, after all.

My feline friend Kiboo is not “my” cat. I think pet ownership is slavery, and I am part of the problem. We’ve created an urban environment of learnt helplessness, and the only respite I feel is that it is herculean to get a cat to do something it doesn’t want to do. We all deserve to be scratched for what we’ve done to animals with speciesism.

I would like to think Kiboo is not my baby or insert infantilised endearment, but a lump of loaf that, against all odds, likes living with me. He is a cat who has entered into a mutually beneficial housing arrangement with me. He has the emotional range of a teaspoon and shares one brain cell with a Bandra landlord. I feed him and house him, and he chooses to sit on my balti (which is what I call my uterus) when it leaks. A good monthly trade-off, even with the poop scooping.

While the Supreme Court was issuing orders to capture Delhi’s stray dogs and put them in kennels and overflowing shelters as a way of “tackling” rabies (another bench walked it back eleven days later, after a very loud week), Bombay was quietly demonstrating what street animal control could look like.

Street initiatives and NGOs, working with the BMC, have carried out trap-neuter-release programmes to sterilise and vaccinate the city’s dogs. The effort has made Bombay an example for the rest of the country. By 2024, a BMC survey found that street dog density had fallen by more than a fifth since 2014, and that nearly two-thirds of the city’s street dogs were sterilised.

Now, when you meet dogs in Bombay, you see the familiar ear notch, an indication that they’ve been sterilised. The dogs are mostly bark-and-no-bite.

Cats, meanwhile, are a different administrative nightmare. They are infinitely more difficult to trap, which makes sterilising them on the same scale a rather more complicated proposition. It is easier to get Modi to do a press conference than to trap a cat in Bombay. In 2022, the BMC admitted it had sterilised about 5,700 cats since 2019. In the previous two years alone, it had done 33,166 dogs.

Which means that while the dogs have been systematically sterilised, the cats remain largely outside the machinery of population control.

And the cats have noticed.

Along with the BMC. Officials told the Free Press Journal that cat numbers were climbing in exactly the areas where dog numbers had fallen. “It is a natural phenomenon,” an additional municipal commissioner said. “If dogs are fewer, then the number of cats increases.”

With the dogs no longer the street’s undisputed muscle, the cats have realised they can move in. They have taken over the streets of Bombay in a way Kiboo could never.

On my way back from work to have a glass of wine at a nearby bar tonight, I saw three testosterone-cheeked alpha male cats perched on a stone wall, chilling next to each other in a way I thought impossible in urban nature. Yes, that is a term I am liberally using. No, you are not required to forgive me.

These three grown bouncers have better boundaries than most men. More importantly, they don’t own podcasts. Yet.

The cats have realised that the common enemy has been defeated without their having to lift a single paw. They just waited these fuckers out.

Now the cats get to chill on ledges, eat food outside meat shops, and procreate, procreate, procreate. Nobody’s mother is asking them when. The cats have won.

They have effectively learned what India should have learned after independence. Once the colonisers have left, you must learn from cats the art of coexistence. Sit on a wall, eat well, always remember who the real enemy is, mind your own business, and be the absolute piece of shit you want to see in the world.

entry.title: Ettina Bhuja Hike
entry.content:
Ettina Bhuja is a cozy hike located in the beautiful town of Sakleshpura, a small hill station located around 230 km away from Bengaluru. Its name when translated to English means "Ox's shoulder". This is because the peak, when viewed from a distance, looks like a bull's hull.

The reported trail length ranges from 3-3.5 km (various websites) to 4-5 km (official Karnataka government signage). It's mentioned to take around 3-4 hours, but if you are even mildly fit, you can complete it much faster.

Hike is only allowed to start between 07:00 and 12:00. And hikers must exit by 16:00. We were running late by an hour and hence reached at the basecamp by 13:00. After loads and loads of requesting, the forest ranger reluctantly called his superiors for permission and we lucked out! This could be an one-off case though. If you are planning to do the hike, it's better to reach in time :). One really good side-effect of us being late was, there was absolutely NO ONE on the trail. It felt like we owned the hike and made sure we made the most out of it!

Hike

Base camp

The hike starts from Sri Nanya Bhairaveshwara temple. Parking spots are available just opposite to the temple. Remember to carry cash, there didn't seem to be any network coverage present here for online payments.

Our destination peak is easily visible from this point but at the same time, it seems super far away. I remember the first time we saw it, we asked the rickshaw driver if we could actually make the to-and-fro journey in just 3-4 hours. That feeling of the peak being impossibly far away will be consistent throughout the hike.

From here, we walked half a kilometer to reach the "base camp". This seemed to be a small property owned by a family providing daily meals, tea, coffee etc. Right next to it, is a small forest ranger shed. This is our actual starting point.

Officer house

There are a couple of checks and procedures one needs to do before starting the hike:

  • We showed our pre-reserved official website tickets. Again due to poor network connectivity, it is recommended to download these PDFs beforehand.
  • We registered our names, mobile numbers, emergency contact numbers, blood groups and a few other details.
  • We kept our bags and any loose plastic bottles in the shed.

The hike is divided in roughly four sections:

  • Walk till the foot of the mountain
  • Lush green jungle
  • Grassland
  • Rock climbing

First section, flat walk till foot of the mountain

First section starts immediately after the signs we saw above. This section resembled a light walk in the park. Whole path is surrounded by trees and flowers on all sides. You would definitely see a lot of beautiful butterflies and sometimes rain-felled trees too xD.

Past the half point, we encountered a stream of water flowing down. We were already feeling at ease after the escape from scorching sun near the shed. Seeing this stream and hearing the sound of flowing water up ahead made us super hopeful for a bigger river/stream! We all rushed forward, just to realize it was all flowing from a water pump 🤡.

We also realized the sound of flowing water was coming from somewhere else. Sadly, we couldn't pinpoint exactly where. In fact for the rest of the hike up, we kept looking for a river/stream but didn't find any :(. This section ends at the foothills, where the trail turns moderately steep.

Second section: walk up the mountain amongst amazing jungle

I would call this section "Bhool Bhooliya" (for non-Hindi readers, read this word as maze). Reason being the amount of confusing two-ways you would notice here. I was able to capture a few of them!

It's important to keep an eye for the signs placed by forest department on various trees, lest you want to get lost in the beautiful woods.

At one point, I took a halt at a two-way and just stared into the woods. Without anything particular in focus, I suddenly felt at absolute ease. I have no clue why I found the otherwise monotonous woods suddenly interesting. While writing this I realized, I sound like the stranger who walked into the snowy woods and just stood still. Breathing in the chills from the flakes, and lost in his thoughts, only to be broken into reality by his horse. I am talking about the man in beautiful poem by Robert Frost, Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening. In that moment, I felt like I was the man Frost talked about. In my case, I was snapped back to reality by my friends.

Forest kept getting denser and more beautiful. We came across multiple fallen trees. Some were covered with moss, some with mushrooms 🍄‍🟫.

I LOVED this mushroom overgrowth. I guess technically they are growing on a dead tree as a fungus, or maybe tree died because of mushroom overgrowth? I am just blabbering here like it is my personal weeknote. I should have asked these questions right then and there cause I was doing my hike with a bunch of environmentalists. This bunch was serious enough to do a PhD in it! Well, in my defence I was lost looking at these mushrooms from different angles 😂.

As we approached near the end, sky and ground opened up simultaneously. There is still a small steep part left to conquer, but from here on out, we could start seeing the peak. We had hiked far away since the first look at the peak, but it still felt so far away! I only realized that was not true after actually reaching the peak. Once we crossed this section which welcomed us with purple flowers all around us, we reached the small grassland section.

Third section: walk through the grasslands

OPEN! We are out in the open! We suddenly suddenly felt the chill of wind and clouds. We could start breathing clouds from this section onwards. There's also the majestic hull standing tall in front of us. And around? A storm of butterflies, beetles, dragonflies dancing around the small grass with flowers all around. HEAVEN.

Up ahead we started getting a glimpse of surrounding mountain peaks except the part hidden behind the hull peak. On our way back, we just took off our tees and lay there. The feeling of dew laden grass on your bare body is unbeatable!

We looked back at the forest we just crossed, and could spot the base camp and temple easily.

We also saw a SUPER HUGE blue and black pattern butterfly here, it was SO BEAUTIFUL 🦋. I have never seen a butterfly with those vibrant colours and the bonkers size before. All of us were mesmerised and spent a lot of time trying to get it on camera. Sadly, the insect seemed to be camera-shy.

One advice I would give to hikers: take some rest here, do not rush off to the next section. It's better to catch your breath, re-hydrate and then move forward cause in the next section, you are going to be doing some rock climbing. 🧗

Fourth section: super steep, V0 rock climbing section to the top

This will be the riskiest and most tiring section of the whole hike. It's a super steep section sitting at around 70-80 degrees. Terrain suddenly changes from small grass to all rocks around. And to get to the top, you have to climb these rocks. You better have good shoes if you are climbing here in monsoon. One slip and you will touch the heights of the heaven.

I was the one to take lead here. With all my rock climbing experience, I carefully guided and supported my friends to cross this section. Btw, do remember to look back at the grassland from above, it looks beautiful :).

Top

This gruelling and slow climb rewards you with a soul healing experience. THE TOP.

Doesn't this photo give vibes of the painting where a man is standing on a hill top with a cane looking over the mountain range?

If you could breathe clouds in the grassland, here you would get slapped by them. The cliff face had winds blowing up at high speed carrying clouds with them. It would be fun to stand there for exactly 2 seconds after you just reached the top, any more and your frozen statue might topple down the cliff face 🥶.

Views from here were stunning. As it was a bit cloudy, we couldn't see the whole mountain range as shown in many of the web search photos. But there was enough visibility to just see immediate hills around. Some were completely covered in forest. Some were grasslands to the top. This left-right variation confused me, but it was also beautiful to look at.

Me and my friends just sat there without speaking anything for half an hour. I appreciate them for this cause few other friends groups I have done hiking with start playing songs on the top section. I HATE that. Rest assured, I haven't hiked with them since :).

There was no noise except the winds, and....a HUGE ASS beetle who had taken a liking to me. Buddy was following me everywhere 😭. I was genuinely so scared, I had considered running down the rocks I just came up on. Thankfully, after some shoo-ing and hide & seek, buddy flew down to grasslands.

I wished we could stay there for longer, but even I had "miles to go before I sleep". It took us 45 minutes each way and that's it. I am not sure where their estimated time of 3-4 hours comes from. 🙃

Loads of flowers

There were a lot of lovely flowers all over the trail. Sadly, I only thought about taking their photos much later in the hike. I photographed only a few, but they are beautiful 🌸. Especially these purple ones, they were all over the mountains!

Pre Hike

Few words on how to prepare for this hike. One needs to book tickets for this hike on Aranya Vihaar 10-15 days before the hike starts. I am not sure on how late you can push this, but its always better to book it early :). Another thing to note is there is a 100-hiker limit. Meaning only the first 100 hikers to reach are allowed to the peak in a day. So if you're going during a long weekend or busy times, you should aim to start the hike as early as possible. Another important point which I mentioned in the early parts of the blog, this is a place where you might not get any network coverage, so it's good to download tickets beforehand.

Arrival

To reach Sakleshpur, you can board a train or a bus in the morning or the day before. It is approximately 230 km away from Bengaluru and from there, the base of the hike is nearly 30-40 km away. Considering the 100 person limit, etc. it's better to reach the night before and talk with a rickshaw guy then itself for the next morning.

We didn't find any modes of transportation to take us near the base camp temple except a private rickshaw. As of September 2026, the rickshaw driver charged us 1600 rupees for the to and fro journey.

Hope you have a good time hiking, till next time, chao!

entry.title: Messaging with Reticulum and LXMF
entry.content:
The first kind of application you could try after setting up Reticulum, or with it, is messaging. I think Reticulum protocol designer Mark Qvist knew that without a practical example of the protocol’s use, people might not use it. Messaging seems obvious.

LXMF (Lightweight Extensible Message Format) is a universal messaging protocol built on top of Reticulum. It’s a distributed (doesn’t need an account with a service provider), secure, versatile messaging system. It also supports store and forward (Propagation Node), so you can receive messages even when you are offline. It can also handle non-text messages, meaning you can send and receive MessagePacked data fields. For example, you can send telemetry, sensor data, etc.

There are quite a few apps. The quality of apps differs. They are all still evolving. Give them six months to a year; you’ll definitely see some good apps. At present, Desktop apps are generally better than mobile ones.

Some apps to try

  • Sideband – Built by Mark Qvist, available on all platforms, including Android (Sideload). It feels more like reference implementation but it works. I use it for all my testing.
  • Meshchat – A well-designed web browser app. It has lots of features. It works vey well.
  • Nomadnet – It does more than messaging. It’s a CLI.
  • Ratspeak – It’s designed well. Available for all platforms including Andoid (Sideload). I found some rough edges but otherwise good.

Don’t run the same Reticulum identity on two machines. The LXMF identity is tied to the Reticulum’s identity. So messages will land in one of them, and they may not arrive in order. It might confuse you. Also, since the identity is attached to Reticulum’s, you can either attach the messaging apps to an already running rnsd or let them run their own rnsd instance, depending on your needs. I usually suggest running the messaging application’s own rnsd and identity. That way, there is less setup to do.

Text is okay; what about calls? It’s possible, though it depends on your Interfaces that carry the packets. But Reticulkum community has LXST, for both voice calls and PTT. It supports OPUS and Codec2 codecs for voice. I have been able to make calls. But I prefer leaving voice messages. I choose Opus Low/Medium quality.

If you like to leave a message or chat. Contact me at my LXMF address : 0b1c6b8c0cfa77f7892715e130f49e66

You can read this blog using RSS Feed. But if you are the person who loves getting emails, then you can join my readers by signing up.

entry.title: An Interview with the Inner Critic
entry.content:
I have discovered that I believe in the Intelligence Value System. In this value system, it is not that the brilliant are more worthy, that is easily refutable. Take anyone you love who is not a genius. They are obviously of great worth to you. No, in this system, the brilliant are afforded certain special privileges just by virtue of being really smart. Among these privileges is the ability to tear down and humiliate whoever they wish with impunity.

I am definitely playing it under the radar in life because of some trauma. I want to stop this, and just live my life following my avenue of interest or avenues of profitability. I want to be able to pursue brilliance without feeling like I have strapped a boulder on my chest. There are many reasons for this. I believe strange things.

  • One of those strange things I believe is that people smarter than you will, and can, tear you apart, and that your defence is to be smarter than them.
  • They will make you feel like you are nothing. But the important thing is that they get to do this. Tearing people apart with impunity is a privilege accorded to them, by virtue of their superior intelligence.
  • Your defence against this is to either become smarter than them, or disengage totally from their realms of intellectualness.
  • The only way to achieve hard goals is to become a hard kind of person who hyper focuses on a thing to the exclusion of everything else, and is rude to others and this is justified in pursuit of their goals, because they are special. Because they are smart.

One of the many ways trauma has affected the second half of my twenties is that I am looking at everything, all information about the world, through its lens. This is just like how I spent my teens looking at the world through the lens of romance, or a lack thereof.

I wish to remove these glasses, and look at life and the world a little less encumbered, a little more objectively, and if that is not possible, at least a little broader out than I can see today.

On the one hand I believe I won’t amount to much in life unless I climb out of this mental model of strapping a boulder to my chest and staying under it, which doesn’t let me learn. If I tell myself I have to become the inventor of GAN or that I am not good enough, I’ll never get this, what’s the point, etc - I can never learn and actually improve. It is like blinding myself mentally with hate. You cannot see ahead or think clearly with all that hate.

Self: “Why do I have to become the inventor of GAN?”

Inner Critic: “Otherwise, what’s the point?”

Self: “The point is to learn about something you are curious about. Expand your skillset. See if it interests you. Improve your confidence. Maybe get ML jobs later instead of being afraid of it.”

IC: “Oh you really believe this crap? That you are honestly curious about ML?”

Self: “It is true that ordinarily I’d steer clear of such hard sounding subjects (all thanks to you). But yeah. I genuinely want to learn about it, because it is dominating tech conversations today and I don’t want to live in ignorance. I want to know what all the hoopla is about so that I need not hide under a rock and hope the conversational spotlight turns the other way whenever AI/ML comes up. Additionally, I would like to inform you - I no longer iwsh to believe the idea you have planted in me that hard things are not for me. It is really limiting, insulting and belittling. Fuck you. Hard things are for me. Easy things are not for me. I get existential crisis from trying to limit myself to mind numbingly boring books and from avoiding hard things. Fuck you again.”

IC: “Well. How do you plan to continue this high and mighty attitude when the going gets tough, like within an hour of your education probably for yo. You are all talk.”

Self: “It is true that in the past I have when stuff got hard. Thanks to you again. First of all, I did not know how to overcome the failure. I thought something was wrong with me - I am an imposter and a failure - for not getting it the first time. I did not realize that I have to sit with the content, go over it multiple times, practice spaced repetition till it solidified in my mind, or come at it from a different angle to grasp it better. I hadn’t yet read “A Mind for Numbers”. I also hadn’t yet identified you, Critic, as the reason for my negative thinking - I genuinely thought something was wrong with me and I should concede defeat. But now, I know you exist. I know you are very powerful, and have honed your muscles and weapons with years of training, haven’t you? I know I’ll have to watch out for you. Journal about you, go to therapy, fence with you like this (Thank you Dr. David Burns), and climb out of any pits you manage to push me into, if not fall into them in the first place. It is sad that I have to do this just to have a real chance at learning stuff, which I am sure comes naturally and easily to many, but I do not care. Everyone has their own demons. You, are my demon. And I have seen you. I will come at you, with all the facilities I have. And I’m sure you know that I can be quite resourceful.”

Demon: “This is all you do. Talk. Even about tech. You do not go for the content, do you. You go for the metadata. The articles about the content. You people-watch and read blogs and convince yourself this means you know things. You don’t actually learn, or put in the work. You are like those people who report on the greats, always in the sidelines. Pink collar journalism at best. Like a Gossip Girl for tech.”

Self: “This is true. It is of no importance how great others are, or if I’m matching up to them. After all, I don’t know anything about this topic now. Whatever they can do to me, tear me apart with their scalpel of brilliance - they can do now. I needn’t care about them and register them as a threat. What protection do I have right now against it happening now anyway?”

Demon: “Obscurity. You are safe if no one knows you. They cannot criticize and belittle you. You need not demean yourself by rolling over and showing your belly to their arguments. You can refuse to engage. If you do not learn, you do not become smarter - but you remain safe. You’ll never engage with smarter people, and they do not get to actually prove and expose to the world how stupid you are. How useless and nothing you are. Like I established earlier, you are never going to rise to their level. It requires sacrifices you are unwilling to commit to (I am being charitable here, assuming that this unwillingness is a choice). If you do not rise to their level, you have no protection against these arguments, their undoing and exposing of you. It is either “roll over” or “be annihilated”. Since neither option sounds appealing to you, I suggest that you do not play their game. Do not engage with the greats. Remain in your lane of midwit intelligence. Have the same sapless arguments, satisfy yourself with an occasional smart turn of phrase. Like you have admitted yourself countless times, there are many blessings in your life - happiness, love, everything you have ever wanted. Focus on that. Mastery is not your cup of tea. Intelligence is not for you. If you do not heed me, you will burn. You are not one of them. You are not a hard person. You don’t like hard work. You like soft things. You will never give up all your comfort to rise to their level of intelligence or hard work. You are not competitive. You are not type A. You are as easy going as they come. You are not high status. You are a bit mediocre, aren’t you. You don’t want the crux of the hard problems.”

Self: “I don’t even know where to begin. Let me go slowly and carefully. I am not happy in obscurity. I cannot believe I thought the hiding strategy would ever work. Perhaps this was your idea. I am quite unhappy in ignorance. I want to learn things. Just now, I do not think this is an intelligence issue at all. Maybe a hard work issue, but not intelligence. Because I have observed that I am good at things I want to do. I genuinely get depressed if I am not working on a goal. I want to be able to go after intellectual goals with all that I’ve got.

Now, more to your point - smarter people exist. People with more knowledge, accomplishments, achievements, mastery, hard work, exist. I have so far refrained from any real presentation of my opinions on controversial subjects to stay away from their fire. But say, that in the course of my life and my education, or by virtue of ever expressing an opinion out loud or online, I come into contact with them, and am engaged in discussions with them. Say, they are tearing my ill cooked observation or opinion apart and I cannot think of a viable defence. Say I am stumped. Say everyone sees this. What really is the fallout from this? They are smarter, my argument is flawed so I’m stupid? Now everyone knows I am stupid and pretending and worthless? And I should just go live under a rock or kill myself or “stay in my lane”? I should somehow minimize myself? And also I should from now on defer to them, trust their opinion more than my own and live my life by their command? This is peak trauma-speak, Demon. I have lost an argument. I have not sold myself into captivity to do the whims of their superior intellect. I am not the spoils of the argument, they are not my captor. There is something else entirely going on here that this is the mode of thinking we have taken.

People lose arguments all the time. I can disengage any time I want if the other person is a jerk or a jackass. I need not suffer obnoxious assholes. This is a thing I get to choose. If the other person is genuine but simply autistic, I can still disengage. After all this trauma thinking really, I do not give a crap. I can do what I want. If the other person is genuine, great. I can learn. I can indulge.

In the past, we have let others argue us into corners, reason about why we should do the thing we don’t want to do; where when we could not refuse their point or articulate clearly why it is that we still do not want to do a thing, we have accepted their argument as a reason to do it, against our own deeper instincts. We are no longer going to do this. We can do what we want. And if anyone is asking us to justify ourselves as to why don’t want to do a thing, we can simply say no. We need not explain ourselves constantly.

Regardless of the other people and their attributes, I am not stupid or pretending or worthless if I lose an argument. This is not a matter of ego or worth - at least it shouldn’t be. I should work on it if every argument I have is devolving into an ego fight, which it isn’t now, so we shall cross the bridge and so on.

What is the expectation here? I should win every argument? People more brilliant than me have the right to tear me down or bully me into things I don’t want to do? No. They are just arguing. This is a discussion. This is safe. No one can do anything to you now. Your self is unharmed and out of the picture. You are a grown adult now.

You need not live in fear. Say you work for an insanely brilliant but obnoxious guy. Say Steve Jobs. He’s giving you one of his stares. You are withering. He’s saying your design is bullshit. He’s going off - “Are you an idiot? You are a dishonest liar. I can‘t believe I employ such incompetent people who cannot bring themselves to give a crap about what they do” (but way more incendiary). Say you whimper internally.

Now, shitty as the situation is, you get to choose. You get to decide whether his obnoxiousness is worth working there for you; Whether you want to take it and then write “The day Steve Jobs yelled at me and enlightened my life” type articles or the more probable “Fuck you Steve Jobs. You may be you but I don’t need this crap” rage quitting that your flavour of trauma would make you do (at least after some examination of the matter with your therapist).

The point is that you have a choice here. Saying “I will live under a rock forever and not learn much and never grow out of my current level of competency and work on my complacency because I’m afraid that one day some guy who is smarter than me would yell at me and make me feel bad if I expose myself to any sort of real/brilliant work” is most mind fucked thing I’ve ever heard you say honestly. And you are the master of mindfuckery. This is the stupidest idea you have managed to come up with so far. Bravo. Is this why you think we need to be absolutely perfect and invent something like GAN? So that we never lose any argument and therefore never need to face any humiliation, and no one can tear us apart and no one can make us feel inferior and then finally, we’ll be safe? We can just breathe easy and just be? You want to be perfect so that you are beyond reproach and since you know we cannot be perfect, you just want to hide away so that “no one can get me”? Oh Demon. You are just afraid, aren’t you. But no one can pick on us now. We are grown. We are big. We can take care of ourselves just fine. We are not vulnerable anymore. We did stupid stuff before. We can say No now. We say No all the time now. I’ll protect us. You are just afraid, aren’t you.

Demon Gargoyle: You say all this. But the truth is you (we?) are just incompetent and will never get to the core of the work anyway. You just do the sidelined shadow work. Remember your school project?

Self: I was 11 and my life was falling apart. I had to cut out my raincoat to make that project.

Demon Gargoyle: You are just conceited. What about that time you knew you weren’t invited to that program and went anyway and pretended?

Self: Look. Everything before college that happened, just be content that we got out of it without developing an intravenous drug habit and a matching STD. Nothing else matters.

Demon Gargoyle: Excuses. But yeah. Leave childhood. What about 5 years ago? You were supposed to research X and you did such an incompetent job. You still can’t do Y.

Self: Yeah. I agree. That’s exactly why I want to learn more. Do you want us to be stuck in “this incompetent land” (in your words)? I know a few things well and I struggle with a few things. Learning, especially with you sitting on my head, is hard. Just let me learn please. Let us improve.

Gargoyle: Yeah. Okay

Self: Okay. I know you’ll pop up again. I am starting to think your intention is to protect me, though in the most fucked up way. Maybe I’m wrong? Idk how you developed. idk your purpose for existing. Whatever. But we’ll talk. I’ll take care of us.

Gargoyle: Okay. Learn.

—

Wow. This inner critic gargoyle was trying to just protect me and in the process, hurting me deeply. Is it, my gargoyle, a maladaptive coping mechanism? I am stuck in mediocrity (or status quo - basically stuck where I am when I know I can improve, because it is afraid we will get hurt if we are not perfect. My demon transformed into a Gargoyle. You know what Gargoyles do, don’t you? They guard.

I don’t know if this revelation will stay with me. But I wish it does. I’ll work on it.

—

About having to be super hard as a person and lose your softness and silliness and playful animalness if you want to become super brilliant: The goal is first and foremost, to improve myself, it is not “Become super brilliant” anymore. That’s the Gargoyle’s goal, not mine. That goal was there so that no one can tear us down or harm us. But no, I'm there to make sure no one can harm us. The mirror image of the “super brilliance” goal is the “stay under the radar” goal. This is also the Gargoyle’s goal. The Gargoyle’s job is to guard us from bigger scarier people who can tear us down (in its words). It can do so in two ways. Way 1: Become perfect. That failed. Way 2: Don’t try anything. So, it was doing way 2. Don’t come under the radar of the brilliant or the privileged (since they are the ones who can tear us down), don’t fail at anything so you never have to face how imperfect and normal you are. Hide. We are not doing that either. We are doing what I want now. And I will protect us. No one can touch us today, and we are neither perfect, nor stupid today. In fact, my intelligence doesn’t have to do much at all with my ability to protect myself and stand my own as a person. It is my independence and general adultness and our sense of belonging that does it. This intelligence as armor is no longer needed. We are well armed just as we are now. We should have been protected when those bad things were happening to us. The Gargoyle shouldn’t have had to come into existence. But we are big now. The arena has changed.

I feel now a deep sense of compassion for my inner critic Gargoyle. I understand why it did what it did. It is small and it wants to protect. How heartbreaking that I wanted to slay it and thought of it as a demon and a devil. I accept my Gargoyle, and now I will protect us.

entry.title: The Food Questions Challenge
entry.content:
Yum!

This is my response to the Food Questions Challenge by James, which I really wanted to write about! I love food 😋 So, here are my answers:

#The Questions

#What was your favorite food growing up?

As someone who grew up in Delhi NCR, my favorite food is unironically Naan with a curry like Chole. This is the comfort food that I can eat every day, and I’m craving it as I’m writing this 😭 With some onion and chutney on the side, it’s just heaven 🫶

Another thing my grandma used to make is Chashni Bread (not sure if it has another name?), but it is basically fried bread pieces soaked in sugar syrup! It’s so unhealthy now that I think about it, but will I have it again? HELL YES!

#What is your favorite food that is made locally? (In your region/country.)

Ghevar! This is a seasonal sweet dish that’s just my top-tier dessert. I love this! The best ones are found in Rajasthan, and I recently got some through a friend living there ;) Absolute banger! 10/10 recommended if you haven’t tried it.

#What is your favorite food generally?

I think a full English breakfast has become one of my favorite things to eat over the past few years. It’s got a bit of everything — sweet, savory, protein and carbs. I also really like having some pancakes on the side! 🥞

#What is one food you have had in the last year that you remember warmly?

Earlier this year, when I was in Portugal, I found this sweet called Flan at my hotel buffet. It looked so appetizing and it was absolutely delicious! It just melted in my mouth and I felt so elevated after eating it.

A friend was with me, and we were both discussing how good it was! I’ve never found anything like this in India, and I realized what a privilege it was to be there and enjoy it ;)

#What food do you really want to try?

Japanese convenience store food, especially the stuff you find at 7-Eleven in Japan. I’ve seen so many people talk about it, and I really want to try it myself!

#Do you take photos of your meals?

Yes, A LOT. As you can tell from the pictures above and my weeknotes, I’m always taking pictures of food 😆 I think more than 50% of my gallery is made up of pictures of food and beverages.

#Savory or sweet?

This is a hard one. I do like both but if I had to choose, I’d probably lean towards sweet.

#Spicy or no?

SPICY, YES! I love spicy food but can’t say the same for the aftermath in my stomach 🫠 On top of that, I try to see how much spice I can tolerate (idk why I’m so competitive?).

#Tea or coffee? (Both? Neither?)

Tea, 100%. I’m not a fan of coffee as such but I won’t deny a good one if offered. Tea, though, is something I still find hard to give up on — it’s like a staple for me at this point…

entry.title: a few "late" bloomers
entry.content:
There's a huge bias towards talking about people who were very notable or "successful" when young. So here are some interesting people who came through a little late.

Kevin Kelly

I always admired Kevin Kelly's approach to work (than his actual work, which, while interesting, I haven't engaged enough with). His real notable breakthrough happened only when he was 31 when he was hired by Stewart Brand.

Robert Moses

Not everyone in this list is going to be a good guy. Robert Moses, by all accounts was a terrible person, but I was surprised to learn that before he became a broker of power and terraformed New York, he was just a complete and total failure. He practically wasted away his 20s in the Bureau of Municipal Research, and what he had to show was a failed policy proposal, and a dead-end career, where he struggled with even finding a job. It was a phone call from an old connection that gave him a second wind.

Robert Caro

Not only was Moses kind of a late bloomer, so was his legendary biographer, Robert Caro, and perhaps the greatest investigative writer ever. Yet, he was pretty much a nobody (though obviously a rather competent nobody), and in his words, "plain broke" right until when he published The Power Broker, at the ripe old age of 38.

Shawn Wang, aka 'swyx'

Everybody in the AI engineering world has heard of him at this point. Though I used to enjoy and occasionally read his blogs before his AI era during COVID. I was surprised to learn that before that, he was pretty much an unknown guy. He had a well-paying finance job that he burnt himself out on, and at the age of 30, taught himself to code via freeCodeCamp. He seemed to have a hit a hot streak, that's been going on since. I had the opportunity to meet him in person during AIE World's Fair, and as the most busiest (and likely enormously tired) guy leading the show, he was still super kind and considerate!

James Murphy

LCD Soundsystem is one of my favourite bands. I really enjoyed seeing this interview of his where he said that he was basically a complete failure, playing in bands that went nowhere, and completely coasting in life. Then after some therapy, he realised that he was just not taking any risks, because he was afraid of failure, and wanted to keep up his image of being this smart guy that everyone was telling him he was. His first hit single, Losing My Edge, came out when he was 32.

Rich Hickey

I still consider Rich Hickey's greatest contribution to not really be Clojure, but rather the clear thinking and the philosophy of how to solve problems that came with the talks accompanying it. Turns out, Clojure and all these talks came out of his retirement savings. He was well past his 30s when he became known.

There's a lot of good to be done in the world in many capacities at any age or time, and it's a bit of an ego thing for a person to pay attention to their age for "success." These are all made-up boundaries, everyone dies at the end anyway, so it just makes a lot more sense focus outwardly on the world rather than inwardly about your narrative.

entry.title: Mutual Funds Decoded - From Order to NAV
entry.content:
Mutual Funds Decoded

As investors, we buy mutual funds(MF) from various platforms and receive units. But have you ever wondered what happens behind the scenes? How do these funds operate, function and what processes are involved in managing them?

In Mutual Funds Decoded series, we'll explore about these in detail.

  1. Mutual Funds Decoded - Structure of MF

  2. Mutual Funds Decoded - From Order to NAV (you are here)

A visit to MF office

Capital Mind Mutual Fund held flexi cap unit holder meet in the last month. When I asked if I can visit their office and talk to the team they gladly agreed.

Thanks to Varun Mishra, Head of Operations, for taking time out to explain various aspects of MF process in detail.

MF Orders

There a bunch of ways investors can buy mutual funds as shown below.

On a daily basis, Ops team will monitor all these inflows in real time, aggregate the amount and let Portfolio Manager(PM) know about the available cash.

MF NAV

A 14 step sequence diagram showing interactions between R&D, Ops, PM, Dealers, Custodian & daily timelines on how MF orders gets converted to NAV.

Why PM can't buy directly?

As an individual stock investor, we can buy/sell stocks directly from broker. But in case of mutual funds, the process is more complex.

AMCs enforce a strict separation of decision making(Portfolio Management) and trade execution(Dealing Room).

  • Best execution of trades: MFs deal with large volumes of trades. Dumping a single gaint market order can move the market and result in poor execution. Dealers use algorithmic strategies to break large orders into smaller ones and execute them over time to minimize market impact.
  • Execution Skill: PMs value lies in company valuation, sector allocation, and risk management. They may not have the expertise to execute trades efficiently. Dealers are trained in market microstructure, order routing, and execution strategies.
  • Regulatory Compliance: SEBI regulations require AMCs to have a clear separation of duties between PMs and dealers to prevent conflicts of interest and ensure fair treatment of all investors.

Conclusion

We have seen how money flows from investors to AMCs & how it gets converted to NAV. We also learnt why PMs can't buy/sell directly and why we need dealers to execute trades.
