entry.title: maybe don't coast?
entry.content:
Something pushes you to coast. Very often, a feeling of having been cheated of something. It is the outcome of a game theory negative system. Your job starts exacting more than its bargain. You want to check out of the game, so you do.

But coasting hurts you more than you realize. You spend a large chunk of your time being mentally checked out. You become reactive. In lax systems, which is more companies than we would admit, things genuinely ease up. Your colleagues start taking their problems elsewhere. You start getting fewer mentions, fewer meeting invites. Someone picks up your slack. Usually someone green. Things fall into a natural rhythm, relieving you of pressure and some hours.

But the quality of the baseline amount of time you spend at work deteriorates rapidly. You drag yourself to work. Neutral as you may try to be, your energy is a net negative on the place. Every day, you let life pass by as you alternate between watching your notifications and the clock. Your grip on your work slips, and with it your pride. Your reputation tanks. Your skills start to atrophy. Learning ceases. Unless you are strongly motivated (in the present tense), the coasting will spill into personal endeavours too. You’re not really in it, you tell yourself. This is not you. That you in the past is you. This is just justice-you, here to collect.

But is there really that much debt? Does it come with an end date?

You may not know what else to do. You do not want to keep exchanging your time for less than what it is worth. But overwork is a pendulum. When the prize of that work disappoints, the pendulum swings with a vengeance into the coasting zone. You must resist its momentum. Rest, but do not swing that other way.

Growth and prestige are important yet secondary outcomes of a job. They are primary to your career, not to your job. Think about how you can get what you want and take measures. Your job still gives you money. It grants you stability. Maybe even a title, bits of identity? Pay it back.

You are depriving yourself of attention. You are “bearing” the hours. Without attention, your life shrinks. Each year can be a milestone on the path of where you want to be. When you coast, each year is a bitter reminder of settling. Being less than what you can be.

Coasting stalls this for you. Let each year find you in motion, not adrift in an arbitrary justice game.

entry.title: Why I Write
entry.content:
I’m currently in an ongoing, self-imposed writing crunch, where I’ve told myself that I won’t share any blogposts (and revel in the subsequent attention) until I finish all my drafts. ¶

This has led me to scratch my head and stare into space for hours, at this point. I’ve even stayed up till 2AM sometimes to try and phrase things a certain way; gone back and forth between different wording structures, and even sometimes said, “to hell with it,” and pressed publish right before going to sleep. That last one would be considered maniacal by some people, and I would gratefully agree. ¶

You’re probably wondering why I am doing this to myself. I am too. The short answer is that I don’t know. But you can watch me grapple with the long one below. ¶

I have been doing communicate-y things for a long time. From narrating a school play in 5th Grade to hosting large events in college. I like to put my scrambled thoughts out into the world and see how people react to it. Not all reactions bring me joy, but more often than not I’m glad that the thoughts are out there and not left with me. ¶

I’m sure it was a not-so-gentle push by my parents for me to attend all these oration and debating competitions — side effects of being an army brat — but over time I developed a taste for it. Preparing my words, memorizing them while walking in circles, and then finally presenting them on a stage. I can’t remember if I had an urge to win; in most cases the attention I received was enough. But that is the root of my journey. ¶

Writing was almost always a side-effect. Pen and paper were the omnipotent tools of the school student, and what you wrote with/on them was completely up to you. The 5-mark answers with the blue pen made a semi-permanent callus on my ring finger, and that callus made it easy for me to write for even longer. ¶

One of these essays — one that stuck with me heavily — was Reliance’s Drishti Essay Competition in 10th Grade. A nation-wide event with the promise of great recognition in its advertising. The habit of participating superseded any hesitation to apply, and soon I was sitting in front of an empty page in the classroom with a prompt written in front of me. ¶

"India — Land of Joy"

I don’t remember racking my brain over the prompt much. I just wrote a few long pages about how my dad’s unique profession (did I mention I’m an army brat?) gave me the opportunity to look at different cultures and see how they all thrive and live together within the same borders. I might have written something about how seeing it all shows you why the country is worth protecting, I don’t know. Maybe I should look for that essay again. ¶

I didn’t expect to hear back about the essay, until I did. An announcement followed by much applause in the Assembly Hall. A silver medal received from the Principal. My name was printed alongside many in Reliance Foundation’s Annual Diary that year, and my mom has kept it safely with her as a memento since. ¶

The attention from it all was temporary, as it always is. But the takeaway I had from the event — the one that my reason to write revolves around — is resonance. ¶

I remember hearing somewhere that a casual remark or a passing comment from one person can cause a deep shift in another without the intention to do so. I have experienced moments like these myself, some of which I document here, so I can tell it’s true. And while I don’t always pass remarks as casually as a fart, I can imagine that other people collect unintended snippets from my writing too. ¶

That, really, is my main reason to write publicly. To leave my thoughts in a place where other people can pick them up, read through them, and maybe find something that sticks with them. ¶

And I can tell it works, because lot of the posts here that have gotten love have been ones that weren’t aiming to be read: ¶

  1. My post about lo-fi tech that excites me was primarily a collection/shopping list for me to look back on in the future, but it somehow reached around 40 thousand views per the anonymous analytics. It spawned enthusiastic comments on forums like Lobste.rs and Hacker News, and ended up in people’s inboxes through many newsletters. The post also got me added to Kagi’s SmallWeb, which I’m grateful for,
  2. My letter to my college juniors stemmed from many juniors reaching out to me with their troubles, all revolving around what they were facing in college. The letter was my effort to provide a response worthy of their collective time,
  3. My posts about the protests of July 20th and October 10th were an effort to show dissent in a place where it could reach other people without being forcefully shut down by the State, and,
  4. My weeknotes remain a place where every week of my life leaves a footprint — an evidence that I was there and did something in it — which also happens to give bits of joy to people when they read it and sometimes find their names in it.

Another reason, which that last point brings up, is the urge to archive everything. ¶

I, hopefully like everyone else, worry about death from time to time. In that worry, I sometimes wonder if I might die with some final wise words left unsaid that could have left one last resonating wave. An instance of the Butterfly Effect left undiscovered for the worse. ¶

I can tell this is a little much, because I have sometimes mentioned leaving my domain name or my web bookmarks or my TBR/TBW as a part of my will, and seen people’s eyes widen with an unconvinced, “Sure, okay.” It might be a little eccentric, but I’m the same person who once took a junior’s comment about my writing being “idiosyncratic” as a compliment, so I’m okay with it. ¶

There are other tiny reasons that orbit around these principles too, ofcourse. My public blogging era began because I was sick of my profession and my hobby both being programming, and needed to do something that wasn’t writing code. God might have listened to me too well on that front, because even programming work mostly revolves around writing normal sentences right now. ¶

The other, final, last-but-not-the-least, cherry-on-top reason, is just IndieWebClub. A community that attracts the writers, the tinkerers and the curious. People who keep doing cool new things and like to talk/write about it. There’s always so much to learn and consume, and all of it leads to my wish to write even more and give back. To share my thoughts that came from their thoughts. To talk and laugh and learn. ¶

I hope we, as people, find more communities and third places like that for ourselves. That we find more places to dance and talk and mingle. More places to find other people. Because all writing, even when benefiting oneself, is still for other people. ¶

It’s about 4AM as I write this. Eyelids are getting heavier but I’m also getting slightly hungry. Wouldn’t it be funny if I just post it and sleep? The blog will come full-circle and all that. Fine fine, I’ll edit and post tomorrow. Peace and love. ¶

entry.title: Programming
entry.content:
0:00 / 0:00
music to be played with this post.
&&

It first occurred to me when I tried out Windsurf. This was the old Claude Sonnet 3.5. The AI made a few edits to my code in response to my query, in quick succession. The code was bad, and it didn't work. However, this was enough. I always thought this might happen, and when it finally did, I felt mentally prepared for it.

I knew this was the beginning of the end of my software engineering career.

It had just been about two and a half years since writing software professionally, but really, I had been programming for quite a lot longer than that.

A decade and a half ago, I was already really into technology. The first program I ever shipped was in VB.NET, after looking up a YouTube video to learn about programming. Why did eleven year old me pick up Visual Basic of all languages? Well, I didn't want to do C++, I knew that would be coming up in our high school curriculum anyway. My brother was already learning Java, and I didn't want to learn whatever he was learning. And Visual Basic seemed to have a nice IDE with drag-and-drop GUI assembly. I built a GUI calculator app, and then excitedly recorded a demo of me showing it off, my prepubescent voice grandly reading out the values as it added, divided and multiplied two numbers. It eventually threw an ugly default popup when the types didn't match because I did not bother handling the exceptions.

After this, I was doing a lot more programming in my free time. It was satisfying to learn the incantations that made the computer do things for me. My favourite class in high school was the computer lab, where I, being the precocious programmer whiz would whizz through all the assignments, so that I could start messing around with programs I actually wanted to write. It was around this time, I aspired to be an open source contributor, rather than just a consumer. I discovered...

...Wait. I know what plenty of you are thinking. You've heard this story beat before. He's going to pick up Python, Javascript, C++, read all sorts of books and tutorials, and slowly unearth the history of this field and its pioneers. Dijkstra. McCarthy. Thompson. Kay. Torvalds. Yada Yada. Oh well, looks like he bumped into Lisp. He read Paul Graham. He chose Racket after seeing Butterick's beautiful website on typography and seeing how it was written. Blah Blah. Now he's also a functional programmer. Yakety-yak. He's reading through Alexis King's Parse, Don't Validate and then Bob Nystrom's What color is your function? and then going further into rabbit holes of program design, abstractions, control structures, and whatnot. You know the drill. He watches Strange Loop talks instead of Netflix like any other normal person. He's not going to just be any programmer, he's going to be an elegant programming craftsman. And with such cool programming taste.

He's then going to start an Open Source club in his college. He will get on a student program to work on Git through their mailing list (unlike the heathens using GitHub), getting his patches personally pulled apart by the fantastic Junio Hamano, the lead maintainer. He's going to make friends with people who help pique his interest in distributed systems and databases. He's going to join a group of brilliant Clojurists who then really help him sharpen his axe, and induct him into the brilliance of Rich Hickey's philosophy. He gets blown away by these "greybeards" and thinks of becoming one of them someday. He had so much to learn, and he was on the come-up. Still green, still full of potential.

And then you know how the rest of this beat goes from here. This AI bulldozer comes through, and the rest of the article is going to be this guy pouring out his feelings and processing his grief for how the profession has changed. The craft isn't what it used to be, and the magic, the joy is gone. The skills I have spent years developing all turning into mist, all getting displaced rapidly.

And this is where I stop you and say, hold on right there.

I actually don't care.

All accounts would say I should be the guy that feels something about what AI has "snatched away." Didn't he wax poetic about the brilliance of Clojure not long ago? Now, hardly before he could really climb through the ranks to become a true master craftsman, the whole way of programming was upended right in front of him. The AI (at its best) can write more sophisticated code than him at an unfathomably quick pace. The roles and the career paths that were available to him no longer exist. Yet, I was unbothered.

If not grief, maybe my response could be embracing the changed craft with a certain youthful degeneracy of a Steve Yegge perhaps? Nope, not even that. In fact, by the time I realised it was the beginning of the end, I was already quite casually thinking of all the ways in which I would choose to not be the great programmer craftsman. I, of course, still value the craft, but I don't feel like I'm some God's chosen vehicle for it. All that matters is that my initiatives are able to produce something useful and usefully tasteful for the world.

You see, I thought I was that kind of guy, this boy programmer to craftsman archetype, but it turns out I wasn't really. It was true that I enjoyed all of the things the community I surrounded myself with enjoyed. But sometimes it felt subtly off—like I didn't quite belong—or the way I enjoyed it wasn't quite like how people I looked up to enjoyed it, in rather inarticulable ways. To perhaps use a macabre analogy, it was like a case of a "great imitator" autoimmune disease where I was misdiagnosed.

I don't quite know what the real diagnosis is. I have not yet found the thing to be long-term obsessed about which people say is a prerequisite for doing truly great things. But the pattern I have seen is that moreso than programming, I am really drawn to ill-structured domains of work. A lot of software engineering work is that way, though not all of it. A big chunk of the programming community is about interest and obsessions with programming structures and concepts, something that felt rather pointlessly recursive. Time and time again, I'd go to conferences and work environments where status is conferred based on how virtuosic someone is at programming. This was initially fun, but over time, I felt more and more estranged from this culture. For me the arena was out there in the world around me, and not in the screen. The brilliance and wonder of technology loses its way before it can make it to the average human, and as a result, most technology sucks, and I kind of hate having to touch and use most of the technology available to me.

So where does that leave me? I don't think I'll ever stop writing programs. Quite predictably, I ended up being a rather early adopter of the new way of agentic programming. But it wasn't what ultimately drove me away. Programming won't be my identity, because the world is much bigger than that. Perhaps identifying with a single profession in today's world is simply not my jam. The world is too deeply interconnected for that to be helpful.

entry.title: Results from India’s Chandrayaan 3 thermal probe experiment benefit future Moon missions eyeing water
entry.content:
Before we begin, I’m thrilled to share that Astrolab is continuing to be a sponsor of my Moon Monday blog+newsletter for the third year in a row! 🌙

California-based Astrolab is developing large multi-purpose rovers called FLIP and FLEX for advanced exploration of our Moon this decade and next. The first FLIP rover is slated to fly on Astrobotic’s upcoming Griffin lunar lander. And NASA has selected a FLEX rover as one of its two Artemis crew-capable Lunar Terrain Vehicles, which will be more advanced than the rover driven by Apollo astronauts. Note: All sponsorships abide by my public Editorial Independence Policy with zero exceptions.

Moon Monday update: I’ll be present and presenting at the 10th Global Moon Village Workshop & Symposium in Thailand the coming week. Due to the event being on Monday & Tuesday (October 26-27) and the travel for it, the coming Moon Monday will be off. The next Moon Monday of November 2 will cover updates from the lunar symposium.

Chandrayaan 3 thermal probe lends literal insights into the lunar surface

The Chandrayaan 3 Moon lander carried a payload called Chandra’s Surface Thermo-Physical Experiment (ChaSTE), developed jointly by two ISRO-affiliated institutions SPL and PRL. Shortly after landing, Chandrayaan 3 deployed and inserted the ChaSTE thermal probe almost 10 centimeters into the lunar soil. The probe touted 10 temperature sensors across its length, and took pristine measurements for each sensor-point from lunar morning to twilight. A study published in Nature in 2025 showed how the measurements helped scientists learn exactly how the Sun’s heat propagates downward from the Moon’s surface, which has key implications for the world’s planning of future polar missions scouting for water ice.

ChaSTE’s measurements from Chandrayaan 3’s near-polar landing site of 69°S are unique because earlier heat flow experiments on Apollo missions and most recently on Firefly’s Blue Ghost lander were in near-equatorial locations, thus tailoring to different objectives not related to understanding water ice deposits on the Moon’s poles. “ChaSTE is the first ever in-situ thermal profiling of the Moon’s near subsurface,” said planetary scientist and one of the experiment leads K. Durga Prasad for an article I wrote for Scientific American. ChaSTE sensors noticed a large temperature difference of 50–80°C between the two ends of the probe, showing that the Moon’s near-polar soil-surface is a poor conductor of heat.

The thermal probe’s tip also carried a heater just above it. It warmed up the subsurface soil, measurements of which let scientists determine its thermal conductivity, and from that infer its density and physical properties. Future missions operating at or near the Moon’s poles need to account for these characteristics. Even though the ChaSTE experiment did not directly study water ice, its results have further relevant implications for future missions looking for said watery deposits. The aforementioned ChaSTE study combined multiple measurements and extensive modeling of Chandrayaan 3’s landed geometry, local topography, and actual observational conditions to derive high-resolution surface and subsurface temperatures across the landed region. This result was more accurate than temperatures inferred coarsely from orbit using the Diviner radiometer on NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. It allowed for a conclusion in the paper which proved relevant to future water-ice hunting missions on or near the Moon’s poles:

ChaSTE observations have shown that at high-latitudes, sunward slopes are considerably warmer and poleward slopes just about a meter apart could be much cooler, providing an environment conducive for the presence of water-ice within the shallow sub-surface.
[...]
A relationship between the local slope and expected surface peak temperature has been derived. The interesting outcome is that the high latitude sites with local slope greater than 14° in poleward direction might offer similar environment as polar sites for accumulating water ice at shallow depths.

The ChaSTE experiment thus suggested that the local terrain and slopes play an outsized role in the ability of near-polar and polar areas to feed and accumulate water ice deposits into their subsurfaces. “Temperatures dictate the presence, stability, and mobility of water on the Moon,” said Durga. The paper elaborates:

Modeling studies showed that surface temperatures ranging from 110 K to 114 K [-163°C to -159°C] are suitable conditions for cold-trapping of water ice, particularly at polar regions. It is also suggested that water-ice can migrate to the subsurface due to strong thermal pumping, if the diurnal [daily] maximum temperature (Tmax) is above 120 K [-153°C] and the mean temperature (Tmin + (Tmax-Tmin/π)) is below 105 K. [-168°C] Also, the presence of a dry regolith layer can reduce sublimation rates, potentially burying water ice deposits (due to any transport mechanisms) under a few centimeters thick layer. Such buried water-ice can remain stay put as long as the temperatures are maintained below cold-trapping limits, especially during lunar nights.

Considering that local surface temperatures at the Chandrayaan 3 landing site hovered around -168°C by nighttime, it’s possible that several sizable poleward slopes in the region are host to subsurface water ice. The findings thus lent mission planners more & broader areas to prospect for water ice instead of being limited to the treacherously rocky regions at 86-90°S. From the paper again:

High-latitude regions with larger poleward slopes can also be potential sites for water-ice prospecting for future exploration and in-situ resource utilization. Such sites would be technically less challenging for exploration in comparison to extreme polar sites, but scientifically equally interesting for enhancing our understanding about the water ice quantification, distribution and migration.

Now, exploring high-latitude lunar regions between 70–85°S is still more challenging in itself compared to the relatively benign near-equatorial and mid-latitude regions, especially in terms of temperature ranges, line of sights to the Sun and Earth, terrain, and slopes. But the high lunar latitudes are still not as extreme as 86–90°S. The Moon’s peak polar areas demand 100-meter precision landings and mission profiles optimized for local summer windows in order to survive and conduct long duration missions. As such, ChaSTE’s findings suggest that future missions with relatively lower budgets and moderate risk appetites could still explore water ice in less extreme near-polar areas, or even peak polar sites for a shorter duration.

Towards the end of Chandrayaan 3’s surface mission, ISRO pulled a trick up its sleeve and made the lander hop about ~50 centimeters away; after ensuring that the deployed payloads and rover ramp were all stowed. During the hop, the briefly lit but powerful engine plumes blew away the fluffy top layer of lunar soil beneath. Chandrayaan 3 then deployed its instruments again, providing ChaSTE a chance to study the older, more pristine lower surface strata. Scientists recently published findings that this block was about twice as dense and about five times more cohesive than the topmost strata encountered pre-hop. ISRO described the result as the difference between an astronaut walking on dry flour versus damp, stiff clay. ChaSTE showed that even within seven centimeters of depth, the thermophysical nature of the Moon’s surface changes considerably. These cake-like layers need to be accounted for in the planning of long duration crewed and robotic missions.

The post-hop ChaSTE measurements also coincided with the time of lunar twilight, which takes many hours on the Moon compared to minutes on Earth. During this time, the probe measured sharp drops in temperatures due to increasing local shadows. This told engineers that the local terrain and object shadows affect the ambiance for hardware operations more than the broader region’s environment does. And it told scientists that both local shadows and the distinct nature of inner lunar surface layers contribute to water’s presence, movement, and storage on the Moon. ChaSTE’s unique set of findings are thus relevant for water scouting, drilling, and even oxygen extraction activities planned by future near-polar and polar missions. The probe’s data is publicly available on ISRO’s ISSDC portal for planetary missions.

India’s next Moon mission Chandrayaan 4 aims to bring polar lunar samples. And the follow-on joint Indo-Japanese Chandrayaan 5/LUPEX rover mission aims to complement it by directly studying the nature, accessibility, and abundance of polar water ice on-site. ChaSTE’s work and science results from Chandrayaan 3 at large feed into both missions as India prepares to take another giant leap for its Chandrayaan program.

Related: Science results from India’s Chandrayaan 3 Moon mission

Many thanks to Astrolab and Kris Zacny for sponsoring Moon Monday, and this combined edition with Indian Space Progress. If you too appreciate my efforts to bring you these curated community resource on global lunar exploration and India’s space activities for free, and without ads, kindly support my independent writing as it’s purely reader-funded. I don’t use AI to write a single word and cite everything.

entry.title: (#2026-W42) chai garam pumping kam (+ extras)
entry.content:
I have some news to share with you. The chai flask in my office finally got fixed this week. ¶

For months I’d been pressing the pump flask repeatedly. Four, five, even six pumps to get a full cup of chai. More if the flask was near empty. But now, with a new flask that has an “OK Tested” sticker at the top, I give the pump two gentle pushes and the cup is full of chai. I couldn’t be happier. ¶

So yeah anyway, the rest of the week probably doesn’t hold a candle to that. ¶

Nevermind, it does. I went to my aunt’s this week after a long time, with a cake and some candles to celebrate birthdays and anniversaries that had come by and gone. I got to spend time with my cousins and catch up with my uncle too. And the cake was delicious. ¶

Speaking of cake, I have also been experimenting with sweets I can have that aren’t loaded to the brim with sugar. I had some Jaggery Kaju Katli which was okay, and some Chocolate Burfi which was so good that I probably shouldn’t buy any (because I’ll finish them way too quickly). The current ongoing experiment is a Besan Laddoo that uses plant-based sweeteners, so I’ll see how that goes. I thought normal sugar was also plant-based only. ¶

I spent many nights playing video games with Marathi Gang this week. I was recalling how, when I asked my parents for a gaming console in school, they would give me examples of their friends who only bought consoles once they were working individuals. “Now is the time for you to focus on your studies. Once you have a job, you’ll have the freedom to play games whenever you want.” ¶

It feels a little weird standing on the adult side now, with Steam installed on my laptop and a debit card in my name. The library of games is endless, and so is the stream of recommendations. I’m facing proper paradox of choice, to the point that I’d like to just not game and do something else instead. But I also get to play games with friends from time to time, which is always fun. ¶

Saturday was a day for IndieWebClub. I only realized upon reaching that it was a co-working session this time; nowadays I just buy the ticket and show up. ¶

I helped set up Gautham’s website and discussed many different things with the IndiePeople. There’s always so many new topics to learn about. I’ve made some changes to my own website too this past week — there’s now an option to view individual posts in a non-doodly font, as well as download them offline as PDF’s. The number of regular readers here is a cozy few, but it’s always to give them more ways to read. ¶

Aeishna also brought in the medal stickers for Blogust 2026, which was really exciting. There were so many different designs and achievements. I took a few (including “Particapation” heheh) which I’m proud of. You can read more about the individual achievements in her blogpost. ¶

The IndieDiscussions continued into Tanjore, and then into Samosa Party. After a long talk over chai, the remaining bunch marched on — half-drenched in the rain — to Ondu Plate for softies. ¶

entry.title: A Run to Remember
entry.content:
Originally written on: Sept 27, 2026

After almost a week of fighting the flu, I felt recovered enough to go on a long run in the forests of Avalahalli with a fellow runner. The plan was to run for 2 hours. The first hour flew past (or ran past?) while exchanging life stories. The second half was decided to be solo. 

I was enjoying the quiet and occasional music from my earphones. But the best part of the run was what came next - unexpectedly a pack of 4 indies roaming the forests crossed my path, sniffing something in the route. I thought they were doing their own thing and paused my run to replenish my energy. 

Wait.. was it me or did their gait slow down? Or maybe something was interesting enough to investigate in their path. ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

I resumed my run and I overtook them (smiling all the while, because that’s just how I am around doggos). After a minute when I looked back, I noticed the leader of the pack racing after me. Five years ago, I would have thought this dog was chasing me. Now, I was just curious and a little confused. Turned out that the leader of the pack wanted to take over and lead my run. One of his pack members did the same, while I kept running at the same pace. And I kid you not - their pace was now matching mine!!!

I thought they’re just joining me for a few minutes and will do their own thing - but no! For the next 20 minutes, I was escorted by 2 bois in the front and 2 bois at the back - my own running convoy. Boy, did I feel special! :’) This will definitely go down as a core memory.

I don’t know what was going on in the minds of these doggos, but I have observed this behaviour in hill dogs across the country (wherever I have travelled). They join you as a travel companion for some stretch and then bid you farewell to continue doing that to other travellers who’re en route. I felt included, safe and protected - even though I thought I didn’t need it in those forests. 

Well, I was wrong - around halfway through this stretch, I did wonder if I was going in the right direction and which path to take, so I just followed the pack leaders…

Around 10 minutes in, I crossed paths with a walker in the park who observantly quipped “The dogs really like you, eh?” and without skipping a beat, I said, “They sure do!” and continued with a big grin on my face. Ahhh, the feeling of being chosen by these furbabies! It’s an achievement I’d like engraved on my epitaph.

A brief glimpse of the escort. I was lost in enjoying their company that i didn’t bother documenting it digitally.

Once I reached the fence at the start of the forest, these furbabies looked back, made very brief eye contact with me (or with their kind running behind me) and then turned right through a small hole made in the fence, while I headed left. The last one in the pack, stopped, paused looking down and then looking in my direction and then headed towards the hole in the fence. If I were anthropomorphising, I’d say he was trying to choose between running with me and joining his pack. But I wouldn’t know for sure. 

All I know, with even more conviction now, is that I want running with furbabies a regular occurrence in my life and not just a serendipitous one (although I would never say no to more such spontaneous convoys in the future).

What are your runs-to-remember? All ears to hear from other runners! :)

entry.title: Solo trip to Jaipur and Ajmer
entry.content:
It had been a long time since I travelled solo with a backpack, and even longer without a laptop. I picked Jaipur because I had never been there, and Ajmer for the qawwali, and the plan was to read, write and draw instead of scrolling. My Google Maps list of places in Jaipur has all of them.

Jaipur

Get a guide for Amber Fort, or it is just rooms and walls. Early in the morning, halfway through, I realised I could ask him to slow down or take a pause, and from then on I did. I loved that.

Outside Amber, an auto driver offered one price to take me around Nahargarh, Jaigarh, Panna Meena ka Kund and Jal Mahal. Each fort has its own ticket, and from the top I could see the whole city. We had lunch together, and somewhere between the gates he became a friend, and we had long conversations about staple Rajasthani foods.

I reached Hawa Mahal close to closing time, took a quick walk inside, and sat in one of the many cafes across the road, for a cover charge of two hundred rupees that comes back as food. After an hour and a half with my Kindle and a notebook, the building had gone from simple to new details everywhere, until the lights came on and the whole front glowed.

I walked the old city, then went down to the metro. At the kiosk a man was struggling with UPI, so I showed him how it works. My phone had no network, so I could not pay for my own ticket, and he paid for it, with a smile and no fuss. A stranger bought my ticket because I had helped him with his, and I understood how small favours make a strange city feel like yours.

At Jantar Mantar I shared a guide with a family of two, which cut the cost in half. Without one the instruments are just strange shapes, and with one I got what each measures, the originals and the prototypes. I stayed an extra hour on my own.

The City Palace next door has two tickets, and you can skip the costlier one, which is just a photo-op, and the guide too. I read in the cafe inside, and my plan not to drink on this trip lasted until a beer there.

Raj Mandir, Jaipur’s famous single-screen theatre, was on my list like the forts, so I planned an afternoon around Drishyam 3 there. The lobby is like a grand hotel reception and the hall seats around 900, nothing like the single-screen halls I grew up around.

Food

It started with Laal Maas at Amano, a rooftop place, and the real stars were the breakfasts. Samrat has everything, not just kachori, with jalebi makers working next door, and Gulab Ji Chai Wale, an old tea stall, was full of locals.

Handi looked like the entrance to a kitchen and I almost turned back, but a few words with the waiter told me they knew what they were doing. The Junglee Maas, mutton cooked dry in ghee, was the best non-veg dish I have had in a long time. In between came lassi at Lassiwala, sweet first and salted on a return, chaat at Rahul Chaat Bhandar, coffee at Half Light and Town Coffee, and sweets from Bhagat for Bangalore.

Ajmer

I took the 12015 Ajmer Shatabdi from Jaipur Junction, two hours and a good one for reading, and returned on the 12978 Maru Sagar. The lane to the Dargah is narrow, with shops on both sides and an ocean of people flowing through it.

A man offered to guide me and sell flowers for the Dargah. I knew this one from the Kali Mata Temple in Kolkata, where a similar offer left me feeling cornered, so I set my limit up front, Rs 200 for everything and a Rs 30 kerchief for my head. He took me through the crowd, I said no to every donation, and I came out with a much smaller bill. I still don’t know whether he was a scam or just a guide, but he made me feel part of the city, and with his help I got an auto to the post office.

I bought postcards for friends there, promising to draw on them next time, and walked back to the room. I knew the way to the Dargah, the restaurant and the hotel.

The evening at the Dargah brought the usual scams around sacred places. People followed tourists for a few hundred metres. Then, at the shoe counter, a man from a nearby hotel held up a plate of food and said fifty rupees. I said no. “Ten rupees,” he said. It took me a moment to work out what had just happened. He was not selling me dinner, he was selling me the chance to feed a needy person standing somewhere I could not see, his business mixed up with my charity. A newer scam. I almost laughed, and that was when I knew I knew this place now.

Inside, I followed the crowd to where the music would be and found a place to sit. When the qawwali started I recorded a bit, and after twenty minutes I realised I was watching it through a screen. I put the phone away and just listened. It was peaceful.

Budget

A little under Rs 50,000 for four days. Flights and the train were close to Rs 20,000, and rooms around Rs 15,000 at Keys Lite by Lemon Tree Hotels and Ginger, which could have been less without a room near the Dargah. Autos and Uber came to about Rs 4,000, food Rs 7,000 since I was eating by following my nose, and guides, tickets and the Dargah about Rs 2,500.

Reading

Once that was done I started reading City of Bones so I can round off my Martha Wells “bookgraphy”. After this I’ll pick up Witch King and hope Ms Wells does not publish something in the upcoming weeks.

Work

The new office finally opened this week after multiple delays, and I’d definitely say it was worth it. The new space is probably 3 times bigger than what we had, the layout is much more spacious, and the pantry stays stocked (if you see this Jyothi, I’m joking). I’ve been helping out with the RealtimeKit backend for the past couple of weeks as work on the mobile SDKs was in a bit of a lull. Unsurprisingly I broke something and got to hold the pieces; thankfully this was only to an internal observability system that didn’t cause any customer facing impact. Thanks to debugging from the folks working full-time on the backend the bug was identified quickly, and I was able to submit a follow-up to resolve it. Learning experience and all that!

I saw a new opening in the DevTools team float by on the internal job board that was very tempting, but I’m still not sure if I want to apply and leave the RealtimeKit team. Things are going rather well here, and I still like being a mobile engineer. We’ll see!

I also got a hefty pay raise to go with it, since I was apparently near the bottom of my existing pay band. As is tradition at this point, my mother’s first question after hearing of the news was asking how much of my new pay will be going away in Income Tax then promptly cursing Nirmala Tai’s entire bloodline.

Tangent about tangents

How do people cope with their work just decomposing into a series of tangents? This is a real breakdown of how I started working on a fundamental rearchitecture of the Mobile SDK’s handling of reconnections (modelled after recent changes in the Web SDK) and ended up spending two days doing NONE of it.

Genuinely starts feeling like I’ve actually built nothing of value when the moment I touch it everything starts crumbling to dust. Maybe I’m just being dramatic and having big feelings for no-therapy-in-a-bit reasons. Onwards!

Gaming

entry.title: Thejesh Gangaiah Nagarathna
entry.content:
I have been thinking about writing about my full name for a while, especially after this incident in which an AI hallucinated my full name. Now that I have a post titled with my full name, it should help our future overlords!

Yes, my name is 3 first names. Mine, my fathers and mothers. Apparently, when I was being admitted to school, my mother was adamant that her name should be part of mine. Strangely enough, her colleagues (other teachers and the H.M.) discouraged it, not anyone else. But she persisted. So I got both of their first names in my name. As it was tradition then, they didn’t expand it. So it was only Thejesh G.N. until I got my passport.

For my passport, I had to expand the name. But it only had two columns, so “Gangaiah Nagarathna” became my surname. It continued like that with my other official documents, though it’s not my surname and for some good reasons I don’t like the concept of surnames.

When I went to the US, they wanted a last name. For some strange reason, they want to call you by your last name. So I was “Mr. Nagarathna”. I have missed my name being called so many times. They have also called me “Mr. Thejesh G Nagarathna.”

Now that you know the story behind my name. My domain is actually my official name, “Thejesh GN”. For a long time, I used “Thej” as my online identity until Gmail came and didn’t allow 4 characters. So I moved to gnthej. After I got and moved to this domain in 2007, I started consolidating all my online identities under “ThejeshGN”. So today, most of them use that name. In some places I still use thej. I do own and use thej.in.

Okay, as a technologist, I have issues with how names are handled online. I think the name should be a single text box with minimal validation. But for some reason, everyone online and offline wants to split it in some weird way or have some weird validations. Recently, I couldn’t add G.N as a surname for a flight; I had to enter GN. I don’t have to talk about folks having problems matching their names from PAN to Aadhaar or Voter ID. I recently saw a form where I had to enter “Thejesh Gangaiah” in the first-name column and “Nagarathna” in the last-name column. Yet another variation!

We also decided to continue this issue for the next generation with “Uma Thejesh Anjana” :)

entry.title: [Blog] What’s in a name?
entry.content:
> What’s the story behind your domain name? (Or your government name, or your online handle.) > This post is a response to an IndieWebClub prompt

My domain name is just my government name, Tanvi Bhakta. Tanvi means epitome of feminity - it comes from the root word tan which means body. But that’s not what my mother (who named me) told me :) She said that Tanvi means “of strong body and beautiful mind”. She said it is another name for Parvati, the wife of Shiva.

The story goes that Parvati, a princess, had decided she wants to marry Shiva (and Shiva alone). So she leaves the worldly comforts and climbs a mountain where very little grows and meditates, calling upon him, for days. Amused, Shiva takes the form of a tribal hunter and questions her desire - he says, “O you of such strong body and beautiful mind, what do you want with the likes of a man as crude and uncouth as Shiva?” She is affronted and defends her beloved well, winning him over and ultimately marrying him. It is from this shloka that my name was taken.

My surname, Bhakta, is not typical for the caste I belong to. Most surnames in the caste I belong to have been around for several hundred years - they are the Kamaths, Nayaks, Pais, Shenoys, etc. But apparently, my grandparent’s grandparents were very pious people. They undertook some kind of pilgrimage and established two temples - one off the coast of Kumta, and one in today’s Kasargod. For this deed, they were named “Bhakta” - the devotee.

Today, the word Bhakt is synonymous with an AndhBhakt - a blind devotee. It is (rightly) a pejorative. I used to think about changing my name but I can’t think of anything I would change it *to*. I have introduced myself with this set of syllables for too long now - it is a part of who I am; the syllables have almost lost their meaning as anything apart from my name. Thankfully, I’m able to separate the meanings in my head :)

[insert Ted Mosby calling a bowl a bowl gif]

I’ve also chosen the name Tanay for myself. It means *the chosen son*. Mum refuses to tell me now, but I think it might have been a contender for my name if I had been a boy? I like that it can play with lots of things - chosen by who? Me! Whose son? The son of *the chosen family*. Son? Or maybe Sun? (My favorite element). I like that it has a strong gendered aspect, to mirror my government name. Tanay Bhakta. It fits, and it feels like a version of me that could have existed.

For a long time, I went by the handle padawanjack. When people see it, they instantly make a Star Wars joke. I am sorry friends, I have never watched Star Wars (and I don’t intend to). When I had to come up with an online handle for some dumb site, I had a vague notion that Padawan meant student of some kind, and I thought that Samurai Jack was cool. I wanted to be perceived as a nerd of some kind, and I wanted to learn sword tricks and perseverance in the face of horrifying evil (Aku). Please cut me some slack, I was probably 8 years old and wanted to play flash games.

I also have another handle based on the characters but I’m not going to doxx myself with that one :grin:

Nominative determinism the theory that what something is named can predict what it becomes. I think names are indicative of a wish that the name-giver has for the named, and that can often be an indicator of the environment that the named grows up in as well. Names are often used as a tool for meaning making in the relationships they we come across later in life. Indian names are especially fun because some meanings are very on-the-surface and can be used in all sorts of puns.

I think I’m pretty bad at coming up with names, and it’s a skill I would like to get better at without thinking too much about the consequences.

---

Related: The story of roughly fifty Sanjanas, how their parents decided to call them that, and the secret history of why Indians give their babies the names they do; https://fiftytwo.in/story/the-namesakes/

entry.title: Lens I see the world from
entry.content:
Prompt: What story do you tell yourself about the world?
Time: 45 minutes

Written as part of Indie Web Club Session #36.

The way I see the world underwent a major change in my twenties - like many people I know. But it left some core beliefs behind, through which I now see the world. 

“Every human heartbeat is a universe of possibilities.”

I remember reading this on the internet more than a decade ago and wondering what these beautifully strung words meant. After some digging, I discovered that it was from the book Shantaram by Gregory David Roberts. The author describes how he used to believe that one’s fate is unchangeable but slowly discovered that no matter one’s luck, one has the power to change their life completely.

Out of context, this might seem cliched, like something you’d expect some motivation guru to say. But to me, this quote served as a mantra for the better part of my twenties. 

While I don’t refer to this quote as much these days, one of my core beliefs stemmed from internalizing it:

You always have a choice.

This is the story I tell myself when I encounter the world - that no matter what happens, I always have a choice. 

I know many readers reading this might feel strongly about this and perhaps even disagree. Here’s why I believe and will continue to believe that.

Halfway-way through my college life, I’d started becoming disillusioned with the world - I used to believe that everything happens for a reason, that whatever happens, happens for the best. While that thought comforted me as a ten year old, as a twenty year old it prevented me from taking responsibility for my actions and my power and influence over how the world worked. 

I made mistakes, but refused to suffer the consequences of them by trying to hide behind the veil of “everything happens for a reason’. “If something bad happened, it’s okay - it probably happened for the good. You don’t know what would have happened otherwise.” 

Later in life, I discovered a name for it - rationalization. 

My antidote to unlearn it? The mantra:  You always have a choice.

Repeating the mantra to myself every day (I am not kidding) for I don’t know how many years, was the start of the Roshni you see today.

Today, if I hear anyone say anything on these lines of “everything happens for good” or “what choice did they have” and not pause to examine that statement further, or worse, refuse a discourse on it, it boils my blood. Or maybe it cools it down because it takes effort to not be cold to them, then.

This is not the same as “free will”. That debate is for another day.

But choice? That is different. It is unique to an individual and the circumstances they find themselves in. It nudges you to see opportunities where someone else does not want you to, or does not know how.

When you believe in your core that you have the choice in every situation, you begin to think creatively, act and speak differently - you come from a place of constructive action and power. In order to be able to do something hard, you must believe in your heart of hearts that you have a choice, that the solution exists.

Power may not always look powerful. It may not always be loud. But it surely shifts something in you.

Over time this belief enabled me to take some hard decisions in life - again and again and again, till it became a habit.

It changed how I showed up for myself and people I care about. In other words I took control of the way I was living my life and actively steered it (and continued to steer it) in the direction I would like for it to go.

Lately, I feel I could use this reminder. To start seeing more opportunities and choices.

I feel like I have steered my life well enough in my twenties that I am now sitting on the shore, taking in the views. I haven’t been faced with too many dilemmas lately which made me wonder if I have sat on the shore a little longer than I’d have liked.

Truth is, when I trained my brain to see choices, it was primarily when I was faced with hard situations. I learnt to see choices where apparently none existed. Now, I am learning to create my own opportunities without a “hard” situation being the trigger (and that is a privilege I will surely acknowledge).

I am now learning to embrace the universe of possibilities, be in awe of them and then choose which of these possibilities I want to make reality.

It’s a work in progress.

entry.title: In search of the perfect media experience
entry.content:
One feed at a time.

This post was edited on 24 Oct, 2026[*]

The rabbit hole

A recent conversation in the IndieWebClub Bangalore (IWCB) WhatsApp group about RSS readers and reading habits sent me down a lovely rabbit hole. I found fun new apps, rediscovered a few old ones and, best of all, got a glimpse into how folks at IWCB read. Some of you have fascinating, occasionally hardcore reading habits. I am looking at you, Abhinav.

As I was thinking about everyone’s reading chronicles, I went back to my own RSS reader and felt oddly lost. My setup, which had been working fine for a year or so, felt broken. I was curious about different apps, new ways to organise my feeds and different ways to read. Damn you, neurodivergent brain!

So I ended up taking a fairly drastic step. For the first time in seven years, I have no RSS reader. I have completely stopped reading feeds for now and am letting blogs reach me as they may. This does not include the IWCB friends. I am still visiting many of your websites and reading your words. Sincerely.

Reading as a river

Here I am now, looking for the right RSS reader for this version of me. I know the perfect reader does not exist, but I am looking anyway.

There are some baseline things that I want from an RSS reader:

  • Works seamlessly across Mac, iPhone and iPad
  • Is customisable without becoming a second job
  • Has good UX (very important). I cannot and will not compromise on the joy of using good software.

But the key thing for me is how I want to read. I do not want my RSS feed to feel like another job, with a queue of unread items to clear. I strongly align with Oliver Burkeman’s philosophy of treating one’s reading list like a river that keeps flowing, and I can dip in for the things that catch my attention and let the rest flow past.

My universe

RSS is only one part of my media consumption universe. My MCU, if you will. Yes, I am calling it that now. The whole thing is my personal hellscape. As Bo Burnham puts it, you can get “anything and everything, all of the time”.

There is YouTube, podcasts and news, as well as books and magazines. In reaction to my internal RSS crisis, I ended up unsubscribing from most other media too. Here I am, trying to rebuild my perfect universe again.

Before this reset, this was what my other media consumption looked like:

  • Videos, mostly YouTube: the biggest time sink. I subscribe to what I like, save what I want to watch later, then try to remember to watch it and close the app.
  • Podcasts: my weak spot. I am a sucker for a good narrative, especially on evening walks, while cleaning the house or washing utensils. A good story gives my brain one place to go instead of running in 10,000 directions.
  • News: I follow half a dozen or so publications across general news, technology, sports and more. Of course, they all have their own apps too.

And this still leaves out the books and magazines I read nearly every evening. I may have a problem, folks. The problem is me.

One medium at a time

Until recently, I was using Reeder to bring all these sources into one experience. It did all the things I cared about. No counts, no pressure, just dipping into a river. Lately, though, switching between text, audio and video in one feed has started to feel disorienting. These different kinds of media probably need to stay separate and do their own jobs.

Videos will stay on YouTube; I cannot avoid that. I am also looking for the right podcast app, but that is a separate exploration and a post of its own. Suggestions are welcome!

News will stay news. No one can fix that industry.

A current I might follow

An RSS reader I have had my eye on for a while is Current, which ticks almost all my boxes. It is available on all the devices, has no unread counts, and lets me group feeds into focused streams called “Currents” (you guessed it). The idea of each stream as its own river feels uniquely aligned to what I want.

More than anything, I respect that it has a clear point of view about what an RSS reader should be. The fact that it aligns with my own point of view surely helps its case. I want to try it partly because of that, and whether it ends up becoming the right reader for me is another question.

There is one small hiccup though, Current costs ₹999 as a one-time purchase. I do wonder whether I could recreate the same experience with NetNewsWire.

Whichever app I end up with, I want to see whether I can open my feeds, read something good and leave without feeling behind. That would be a good enough reason to keep using it.

For now, this is me building my media universe again, feed by feed. RSS first. Next up, podcasts.

entry.title: [Weeknotes] Week of October 17th, 2026: Learning while working, todoist overwhelm, and annotated novels
entry.content:
I am simply declaring bankruptcy on the weeks before this. I am also posting this entirely from my phone; maybe this way I will be able to write more.

Work

A few weeks ago I finally figured out how to get the llm to teach me things in a style in which I can learn. Working with llms has been much better since then.

I also hope that I have figured out the balance of using llms without outsourcing my thinking to them. I am doing at least 5 times the output of the work I used to do (pre llm). But I've found that I can care about at most 3 things a day, before my brain gets very, very tired.

I'll have a post up soon about how we're doing evals and what I learnt from it!

Life

My to do list (literally, the app) had somehow become a mix of things I must do to survive + dumb things I don't want to forget. The rest of my everyday tasks stayed in my head. This week, i finally put all of those tasks down in the app too! Instant catatonia. I got so overwhelmed looking at all of it that my brain just started haphazardly picking up things to get done even if it wasn't as important. All my regular self soothing mechanisms were not working. I called a friend, diagnosed the problem, and made several views for myself so that I am seeing smaller sets things in my everyday. But it was a good lesson that I am really just a bundle of systems that work and coping mechanisms.

Last weekend was Maya Bazaar. Got there super late, missed lots of my friends, skipped quite a few performances, but I'm pretty happy that I spent most of my money on stalls belonging to trans folks, and then some rings haha.

Azan did a set in his living room. For his birthday last week he did a very long noodley set that I still have playing in my head. This set was "tighter" but I know he is hiding more songs in his back pocket. Want a soundcloud link.

The rest of the week has been quiet. Didn't even leave the house except for Tuesday dinner. Been sleeping at 8pm where I can and the body has appreciated it.

Health

Still in the flare that started mid August. Getting a little tired of it now. Go away. The last week especially I have wanted to move more, but have been afraid. (Iykyk) Would not wish chronic illness on my worst enemy. Okay wait, i have thought about who my worst enemies are (hint: people have been marching against them!) and maybe I would.

A friend has offered to spend quality time with a bottle of oil and my back. I also hope to play some football this week. Let's see.

Learning

Apart from the recall teach skill i programmed, i finally lost my patience and got a kannada deck made for Anki. I'm having more fun than I have had with it before.

Media Diet

Reading

I wanted something familiar but epic so I have been rereading The Locked Tomb series via this annotated doc. It's like having all the theories in one place outside my head. But using google docs on mobile especially for a big doc is so painful. Unfortunately a lot of the reading experience also comes from reading the comments left on the doc, so I'm stuck to that platform for now.

Listening

Been really enjoying the quiet jazz of Nala Sinephro, especially her Spaces 1.8. Thanks Azan! Jhene Aiko's Westside Whimsy feels like classic rnb, great afternoon listening but forgettable. Having lots of fun with Bangalore ka Potta, thanks Ashlesh!
